title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Interview at The Money Mindset with Sonia Shenoy on February 15, 2025
summary: In a wide-ranging interview in India, Pabrai describes himself as a single-game player, recounts the 2007 Buffett lunch and the lessons it produced (leverage, inner scorecard, hanging out with better people), and argues that know-nothing investors should simply hold a low-cost index because patience beats stock-picking. He walks through the Reysas case (bought at 2% of liquidation value in Turkey, now over 60% of his portfolio and not for sale), puts NVIDIA, Tesla and Palantir in the too-hard pile, and closes with his philosophy of life as a game, the June 11, 2054 'death date', Dakshana, entrepreneurship as low-risk, and hacks for parenting teenagers.

ideas.idea: He is a single-game player who picks games where he has an edge; Pabrai Funds and Dakshana are both games.
ideas.detail: Industrial psychologists tested him 26 years ago and concluded 'he likes to play games'; he plays Bridge, not team sports. Life has no grand meaning, so make the most of a short time and have the most fun.

ideas.idea: Start new endeavors small so failures are contained, then press the accelerator only when there is traction; the failures are what teach you.
ideas.detail: Many of his ventures did not work; the ones that worked taught him nothing, so he cherishes failures and refuses to sweep them under the rug.

ideas.idea: Paying $650,000 for the 2007 Buffett lunch was a cheap 2-3% tuition bill on the $70M+ of net worth attributable to Buffett's teachings, and it turned into 'buy one lunch, get infinite lunches free'.
ideas.detail: He had bid unsuccessfully since 2004; the last lunch went for $26M. The lunch led to a friendship with Charlie Munger, dinners every couple of months and being his Bridge partner at the LA Country Club.

ideas.idea: Buffett told his daughters, then 10 and 12, that the most important decision in life is whom you marry, which needs a balance of heart and head.
ideas.detail: Buffett said he had nothing going on all afternoon and would stay as long as they wanted; he converts every 'lemon' question into lemonade with a lesson.

ideas.idea: If you are even slightly above average, spend less than you earn and use no leverage, you cannot help but get rich over a lifetime.
ideas.detail: Rick Guerin, the third partner with Buffett and Munger, was in a hurry and used margin; in the 1973-74 drawdown he was forced to sell Berkshire to Buffett at $20 a share, now worth ~$700,000, a 35,000x. Buffett and Munger knew they would get rich but were not in a hurry.

ideas.idea: Measure yourself by the inner scorecard, not the outer one; it becomes the baseline for growth because you have no illusions about your flaws.
ideas.detail: Buffett's test: would you rather be known as the best lover in the world but know you are the worst, or vice versa? Knowing the answer puts you far along toward success.

ideas.idea: Hanging out with people better than you trumps loyalty: be a harsh grader of humans and deliberately increase time with the exceptional ones.
ideas.detail: There is a gravitational pull both ways; he does a post-mortem after every lunch or tea to decide whether to repeat it and winnows down to people he truly enjoys.

ideas.idea: Following Marcus Aurelius, to encounter misfortune and overcome it is good fortune; every adversity in his life has led to greater growth, so he now smiles through challenges.
ideas.detail: At almost 61 he says there is no case where adversity did not produce growth; confront it head-on with faith that tomorrow will be better, which means there is never a downside in life.

ideas.idea: If wealth is lost nothing is lost; the US safety net means poor people are fat, so losing a job or a drawdown is not something to fear.
ideas.detail: His father went bankrupt several times with heavy leverage and no savings, so the family relied on friends for groceries and rent; as an adult he put 15% of salary into his 401k from day one to never repeat that.

ideas.idea: Markets go through long flat stretches and long booms; the Dow was 865 in both 1965 and 1982, then rose to ~12,000 by 1999, then was flat to 2012.
ideas.detail: In 1982 Coke and P&G traded at 6-7x earnings. The Sensex since the 1991 reforms similarly shows zero stretches and 18-20% stretches but a tremendous average.

ideas.idea: A know-nothing investor who cannot value a business should buy a low-cost broad index fund via SIP and ignore market swings.
ideas.detail: The index is too dumb to know it owns Google and too dumb to sell it; it will hold Asian Paints, HDFC and Titan for 30-40 years while individuals dance in and out, and it removes the Xeroxes and Kodaks over time.

ideas.idea: The single most important skill an investor needs is patience: if 49 of the US Nifty 50 went to zero and you only kept Walmart at 2%, you still beat the S&P.
ideas.detail: The Walton family owned 36% at IPO and 44% today, 55 years later, with no Waltons in senior management. If you love watching paint dry you will do extremely well.

ideas.idea: Great businesses can be severely overvalued for a decade and still reward patient holders, so overvaluation alone is a weak sell signal.
ideas.detail: He wrote in 2000 that Infosys was ridiculously overvalued and returns were zero for 8-9 years, yet holding to today worked extremely well; Microsoft went from $600B to under $200B and was flat 2000-2012 but is still a 5-6x from 2000.

ideas.idea: Have a heavy bias toward treating everything as noise; do not sell a high-quality business just because it became overpriced, but get off the bus in obvious secular decline.
ideas.detail: Businesses with great moats and cultures have 50-75 year histories, and a stock picker should ride them as long as fundamentals are in place.

ideas.idea: 99% of stocks belong in Buffett's too-hard pile; NVIDIA, Palantir and Tesla go there because he cannot forecast their cash flows 5, 10 or 15 years out.
ideas.detail: Buffett keeps a 'too hard' box on his desk. Tesla's valuation makes no sense on current cash flows, but Elon is constantly underestimated, which is exactly why it is too hard.

ideas.idea: With 50,000+ stocks globally, being flexible and knowing nothing about 99.9% of them still leaves a few hundred where a no-risk, high-conviction bet is delivered on a platter.
ideas.detail: He went to Turkey six years ago because it screened as the cheapest market in the world and a Ben Graham-style friend, now Turkey's second-largest fund manager, agreed to show him only companies he owned, starting with his highest-conviction stake.

ideas.idea: Reysas was bought at a $16M market cap against $800M liquidation value, 2% of value, and is a one-and-done opportunity he will never see again.
ideas.detail: For $8M he got a third of the company in 2019; Templeton sold him 5% for $1M because New York told them to exit Turkey. The lira went from 5 to 36 per dollar, yet market cap is now over $1B and liquidation value over $2B. The founders proved to be creative capital allocators, so the fund will only sell when they sell.

ideas.idea: When the value gap is enormous you do not need to do much work before buying; the detailed study can come after.
ideas.detail: On his Turkey trips he deliberately did no work before meeting companies and only studied Reysas over subsequent years; in Turkey he focused on businesses where currency and inflation are irrelevant.

ideas.idea: The stock market is a theater where every seat must be occupied, so look for theaters with an illusion of smoke rather than real smoke.
ideas.detail: When investors flee a market en masse the baby gets thrown out with the bathwater; that is why he went to Turkey. Most of the time the smoke is real and you do not need to go there.

ideas.idea: Trips to the pie counter are few, so load up in size: Turkey is now 60-65% of the portfolio in just two businesses and he told investors he will not sell.
ideas.detail: Munger says load up on pie because you get few trips; Buffett says when it rains gold put out a bucket, not a thimble. Investors can sell fund units to cut concentration, but the fund will not sell.

ideas.idea: NVIDIA at a $3 trillion market cap is not a trip to the pie counter because it would need to reach $100 trillion, more than the entire US market.
ideas.detail: Auction-driven markets do not offer such outcomes at that starting size; the question for any buzzy stock is whether it is genuinely a pie-counter trip.

ideas.idea: Knowing your expected death date, June 11, 2054, frames the two games he plays: a compounding engine and a give-away engine so that only $10,000 is left the day before he dies.
ideas.detail: He used MetLife's life-expectancy calculator. He could have retired at 33; all wealth since is abstract and will go back to society, echoing Buffett's view that 99.999% of his wealth cannot make him happier. Dakshana, 16-17 years old, must scale to give effectively.

ideas.idea: Less is more: he and Buffett refuse multiple homes, and he benchmarks every activity or meeting on whether it will make him happier.
ideas.detail: Media and advertising tell people to want bigger homes and better cars; he feels on vacation every day and often finds trips worse than daily life. This dovetails with the inner scorecard.

ideas.idea: Entrepreneurs do not take risks; his 1990s startup was a calculated low-risk bet built nights and weekends with bankruptcy law as the backstop.
ideas.detail: At 25 on $40,000 a year he worked 6-9am and 6pm-midnight for nine months on his third startup (the first two lost $2-3K) until cash flow slightly exceeded salary. He lined up $70K in unused credit-card limits and $30K in a 401k, learned personal bankruptcy would wipe the debt, and his bosses promised to rehire him 'when it fails'; both later invested in his fund.

ideas.idea: A life well-lived leaves the planet better than you found it, and being a great parent is non-negotiable.
ideas.detail: Know yourself first, since we come without an owner's manual, then pursue passion: if you would not do your job unpaid it is the wrong job. From The Hidden Logic of Teenagers: after age 12 friends matter most, so drive teens and stay silent to gather data, keep an open house for pizza, talk to them after midnight; he changed his younger daughter's school to break a bad friendship.
